title: El Niño – unusual weather in the Pacific

paragraphs.text: Historical records speak of an El Niño that took place in 1567. We can only guess what earlier civilisations thought of this change in weather, and what gods they cursed for the drought, or lack of fish, or massive rains that wiped out their crops. Peruvian sailors who fished in small boats along the western-most shores of South America were the first to give a name to the phenomenon. Normally the waters they fished were cold, but in certain years the waters would reverse their flow and become very warm. This, of course, was not good for fishing; basically the fish food chain would collapse and the year would be a write-off for the fishermen. Because the phenomenon would usually begin to peak around the Christian Christmas holiday, the sailors named the odd weather ‘El Niño’, meaning the ‘Christ Child’.

In September 1982, scientists and crew on board the research vessel Conrad, sailing eastwards along the equator in the Pacific, first noticed that things were not as they should be. The sea surface temperature was noticeably warmer than it should have been for that time of the year, and the ship’s cook, the main responsible for the food preparation on board, was not getting enough supplies of fish. What is more, a message was reaching the crew from the main computer at Washington DC, USA, indicating that they took were anomalies – so anomalous, in fact, that they were reluctant to reject anything that was happening as faulty measurements, since it was programmed to reject anything that was the result of faulty instruments. Nevertheless, the scientists assumed that such measurements would be the result of faulty instruments, hence ignored them.

Then, a most important thing was recognised when one of the main engines on the Conrad developed a problem. Running on only one engine would leave the vessel considerably behind schedule, since the engine had to work against the prevailing east-to-west current. However, all of the navigational readings revealed that the vessel was travelling east faster than it should have been; the Conrad was actually ahead of schedule. This could only have happened if the ocean currents were flowing from west to east, the reverse of the normal direction. We now know that the crew witnessed one of the strongest El Niños of the twentieth century.

For a long time the unusual appearance of warm surface waters off the coasts of Peru and Ecuador had been thought of as a local, coastal phenomenon, occurring independently of any other weather patterns. In the early twentieth century, however, Sir Gilbert Walker developed a very different theory.

In 1904, Walker, a British scientist, became the head of the meteorological service in India. The 1899 monsoons – the heavy rains expected between June and September – had failed to materialise, causing a famine, and Walker began to investigate why that had happened, and to work out how to forecast the yearly changes that occur in monsoons. Monsoons are sporadic, and they make life something of a lottery. If they don’t come, there is drought, or if the rain is more torrential than usual, crops are destroyed: in both cases, the consequences are likely to be disastrous.

Walker was convinced the variation in monsoons was in some way global in nature. As he and his assistants sorted through weather records from around the world, he associated certain patterns of rainfall in South America with variation in ocean temperatures. He also found a correlation between rainfall patterns at stations on the eastern and western sides of the Pacific. He noticed that when air pressure rises in the east, it usually falls in the west, and vice versa. He also realised that Asian monsoon seasons under certain barometric conditions were often linked to drought in Australia, Indonesia, India and parts of Africa, and mild winters in Western Canada. Walker was convinced that all these events were connected.

Such a claim had never been made before, and Walker was publicly criticised for suggesting that climatic conditions over such widely separated regions of the globe could be linked. He was unable to translate his findings into a scheme that predicts the nature of the monsoons. He conceded that he couldn’t prove his theory but predicted that whatever was causing the connection in weather patterns would become clear once wind patterns above ground level, which were not routinely being observed at that time, were thrown into the equation. He was later proved right. In the 1960s, a Norwegian meteorologist, Jacob Bjerknes, identified detailed interactions between the ocean and the air, and proved that there are indeed global weather systems.
